tip: The ending -ούλα (-úla) makes a word small and affectionate: κοντούλα (kondúla) = petite.
Brown splits in Greek: καστανά (kastaná) for eyes and hair, καφέ (kafé) for objects like shoes – swap them and it sounds off.
Adjective as noun: ο ψηλός (o psilós) = the tall one/guy.
Μοιάζω (miázo) = look like, and it takes σε: μοιάζεις στον πατέρα σου (miázis ston patéra su) = you look like your father.
Έχει ζωή (ékhi zoí) is literally 'it has life' = it's lively – Greek places often 'have' their qualities: έχει κόσμο (ékhi kósmo) = it's crowded.
Τόσο... όσο (tóso... óso) = as... as: τόσο ακριβό όσο φαίνεται (tóso akrivó óso fénete) = as expensive as it seems.
Κλείνω (klíno) = to book, literally 'to close': θέλω να κλείσω δωμάτιο (thélo na klíso dhomátio) = I want to book a room.
Με πρωινό (me proinó) = with breakfast – με usually takes a bare noun for what's included, like με θέα (me théa) = with a view.
Τη βραδιά (ti vradhiá) = per night – no separate word for per.
For a do-it-once command the verb swaps -ν- for -σ-: κλείνω (klíno) becomes κλείσε (klíse) = book!
Μου (mu) usually pulls a second accent onto a longer word: στο όνομά μου (sto ónomá mu) = in my name.
Καλή διαμονή (kalí dhiamoní) = enjoy your stay – καλή/καλό + noun is the standard Greek wish: καλό ταξίδι (kaló taksídhi) = safe trip.
Υπάρχει (ipárkhi) = there is, a notch more formal than plain έχει (ékhi) – both work at the desk: υπάρχει πάρκινγκ; or έχει πάρκινγκ; (ékhi párking).
Πολλή with two λ is the feminine a lot: πολλή φασαρία (polí fasaría) = a lot of noise.
Apologizing is literally asking: μας ζήτησαν συγγνώμη (mas zítisan sighnómi) = 'they asked us forgiveness' – the person wronged is just μας (mas).
The ongoing past form covers a state that lasted: μύριζε (mírize) = it smelled the whole time.
Two past forms, two jobs: φυσούσε (fisúse) = the wind was blowing, an ongoing scene; άργησε (áryise) = it was late, one finished event.
Για δέκα λεπτά (ya dhéka leptá) = by ten minutes – για marks the margin you missed it by.
Περιμέναμε (periméname) is the ongoing past: the waiting stretched on, which is what almost three hours calls for.
Γεμάτος (yemátos) = full of takes a plain object, no word for of: γεμάτο κόσμο (yemáto kósmo) = full of people.
Είχε κύμα (íkhe kíma) is literally 'it had wave' = the sea was rough – Greek often lets the sea 'have' its conditions, with no adjective.
Έδεσε (édhese) is literally 'it tied' – ships dock by tying up, so Greek just says the boat tied: το πλοίο έδεσε (to plío édhese).
Μόλις (mólis) with a finished-action past = as soon as: μόλις φτάσαμε (mólis ftásame) = as soon as we arrived.
Greek stacks negatives: δεν έφυγε κανένα πλοίο (dhen éfiye kanéna plío) = no boat left – κανένα (kanéna) and δεν (dhen) both stay, that's not an error.
Ταξιδεύαμε (taksidhévame) is the ongoing past, the all-night background; φτάσαμε (ftásame) is the one-off event, the arrival that caps it.
Η θάλασσα ήταν λάδι (i thálassa ítan ládhi) is literally 'the sea was oil' – the everyday Greek image for a dead-calm, glassy sea.
Τον δικό του (ton dhikó tu) = its own.
Θέλει (théli) usually = wants, but with a stretch of time it means needs: θέλει μία εβδομάδα (théli mía evdhomádha) = it needs a week.
Γυρίζω (yirízo) means both go around and come back – context decides: γυρίσαμε όλο το νησί (yirísame ólo to nisí) = we went around the whole island.
Δίπλα στο κύμα (dhípla sto kíma) is literally 'next to the wave' – the everyday Greek way to say a place sits right on the water.
